sentences.text: Zupaysaurus is considered a bipedal predator that could reach up to 4 meters in length, though no complete skeleton has been found.
A 2016 study estimated Zupaysaurus to be 4.2 meters long and weigh 70 kilograms.
Zupaysaurus walked exclusively on its hind legs, freeing its forelimbs to grasp prey.
Later analysis identified the supposed skull crests of Zupaysaurus as a displaced nasal bone rather than true crests.
Zupaysaurus possessed a rough lacrimal ridge projecting from the upper edge of its skull.
The adult skull of Zupaysaurus reached a length of 45 centimeters.
Like other members of its class, Zupaysaurus was bipedal.
A small gap between the premaxillary and maxillary teeth in the upper jaw, and the fusion of the astragalus and calcaneum in the ankle, place Zupaysaurus among primitive theropods.
Like coelophysoids, Zupaysaurus had a twist in the snout between the premaxillary and maxillary bones of the upper jaw.
The length of recovered neck bones suggests that the genus Zupaysaurus had a fairly long neck.
Additional cranial ornamentation included a rough lacrimal crest projecting laterally on the top of the skull.
The name Zupaysaurus translates to "devil lizard," combining the Quechua word for devil and the Greek word for lizard.
The fauna of the Los Colorados Formation is recognized as one of the earliest known dinosaur-dominated assemblages, where dinosaurs made up 43% of the known tetrapod species.
Zupaysaurus was discovered in May 1997 by Santiago Reuil and formally described by Andrea Arcucci and Rodolfo Coria in 2003.
The species name Z. rougieri honors Guillermo Rougier, who led the expedition that found the holotype specimen PULR-076.
Zupaysaurus was discovered in May 1997 by Santiago Reuil, part of Guillermo Rougier's team, and was described by Arcucci and Coria in 2003.
The type species was named Z. rougieri in honor of Guillermo Rougier, the scientist who led the expedition that discovered and collected the holotype PULR-076.
Zupaysaurus was first described and named in the scientific journal Ameghiniana by Argentine paleontologists Andrea Arcucci and Rodolfo Coria in 2003.

The holotype specimen PULR-076 consists of an almost complete well-preserved skull, the right shoulder girdle, the lower part of the right leg and ankle, and twelve vertebrae of the neck, back, and hips.
The well-preserved braincase of the holotype allowed researchers to reconstruct Zupaysaurus's brain anatomy using a digital endocast.
Yates (2006) classified Zupaysaurus within the monophyletic family Dilophosauridae alongside Dilophosaurus and Dracovenator.
Zupaysaurus is classified as a dilophosaurid theropod dinosaur.
Zupaysaurus was classified as the oldest known tetanuran theropod due to various characteristics of its skull, dentition, and hind limbs.
In 2006, Yates found that Zupaysaurus formed a group with Dilophosaurus and Dracovenator, placing it in the monophyletic Dilophosauridae.
But later studies found that Zupaysaurus was a sister taxon to a clade containing dilophosaurids, ceratosaurians, and tetanurans.
Zupaysaurus was an early theropod dinosaur that lived during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina.
The original Zupaysaurus specimen dates to at least 213 million years ago from the late Norian stage of the Late Triassic.
Zupaysaurus lived between 226 and 206 million years ago, spanning from the Norian to the Rhaetian stages of the Late Triassic.
Precise dating estimates place the Los Colorados Formation, and thus Zupaysaurus, between 227 and 213 million years ago.
Zupaysaurus lived in an ancient floodplain environment alongside early sauropodomorph dinosaurs such as Riojasaurus, Coloradisaurus, and Lessemsaurus.
The formation where Zupaysaurus was found has been dated by magnetostratigraphy to the Norian stage of the Late Triassic, approximately 228 to 208 million years ago.
The time range for Zupaysaurus is the Norian stage, from 227.3 to 205.7 million years ago.
It is debated whether Zupaysaurus possessed tall narrow crests or merely low ridges along its snout, with later studies suggesting the crests were misplaced bones.
There is debate regarding Zupaysaurus's classification, as it displays features of both tetanuran theropods and more basal theropods.
However, more recent analyses of the skull have cast doubt on the presence of the crests in Zupaysaurus.
An unpublished summary presented at a recent conference indicated that the structures initially identified as crests were actually lacrimal bones displaced upward during the fossilization process.
